newsitem.title: LIBERIA: Taylor waits to be proclaimed president of Liberia.
newsitem.headline: Taylor waits to be proclaimed president of Liberia.

text.p: Liberia's electoral chiefs made final ballot checks on Wednesday before proclaiming former warlord Charles Taylor winner of presidential elections.
Partial results announced on Tuesday night gave Taylor an unassailable lead of more than 75 percent over 11 rivals, assuring him the top job he failed to win by the gun.

One of the presidential contenders, former foreign minister Baccus Mathews, conceded defeat on Wednesday and endorsed the elections as "reasonably free and fair". He called on Taylor's other rivals alleging malpractice to accept the results.
"There were problems but they were not massive enough to affect the result," Mathews told Reuters.
"It's much easier for me to accept these results and go beyond them," said Mathews, a campaigner for multi-party democracy dating back to the days of one-party rule in the 1970s.
Elections commission chairman Henry Andrews told a news conference he hoped to formally announce the winner by Wednesday night -- certainly not later than Thursday, by law.
He said Taylor had not been proclaimed the winner after Tuesday's results as the commission wanted to be sure turnout was as it estimated -- 600,000 from 700,000 registered voters.
Taylor needed 50 percent plus to win on the first round.
However, Andrews added: "Once these figures are released they are official and there's nothing to stop you as journalists to draw your own conclusions (as to the winner)."
Taylor addresses a Wednesday news conference at 1 p.m. (1300 GMT) at his party headquarters.
Liberians looking for strong leadership after an agonising seven-year civil war voted overwhelmingly on Saturday for the man who started the fighting.
The conduct of the presidential and general elections, Liberia's first since 1985, received unanimous endorsement from more than 500 foreign monitors and over 1,000 local observers.
But other presidential candidates, clobbered even on their home turf, cried foul as Taylor's margin of victory stretched with each successive result bulletin.
The results gave Taylor's National Patriotic Party 356,548 votes or 75.4 percent from 472,863 votes counted.
His nearest rival Ellen Johnson-Sirleaf, the only woman in the presidential race, polled 45,195 votes or 9.5 percent.
At a news conference after the results bulletin, Johnson-Sirleaf questioned the margin of Taylor's lead.

"Statistically it's just impossible," said the former senior United Nations official. "These results show strikingly that there's only one candidate who obtained an overwhelming percentage of the votes. It is too good to be true."
However she suggested her Unity Party may still accept the final results, even though it planned to update a petition filed with the elections commission on Monday.
Two other warlords -- Alhaji Kromah and George Boley -- also ran for president but neither has managed to poll even five percent so far.
Kromah, in a BBC radio interview, also alleged malpractice.

Taylor's invasion from Ivory Coast in December 1989 launched the civil war in which more than 150,000 people were killed. The economy is ruined and half the pre-war population of 2.5 million people are displaced.
Liberians voted massively but peacefully in what political leaders described as an emphatic rejection of rule by the gun.
